section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Vectors as Arrows
section_1.content: Briefly define a vector as a directed line segment with magnitude and direction in 2D space. Visualize vector addition (tip-to-tail method) and scalar multiplication as scaling the arrow length.
section_1.example: A robot arm on a 2D plane: Vector 'u' is the reach of segment 1, 'v' is segment 2. Their sum represents the robot's end-effector position.

section_2.title: Linear Combinations and Span
section_2.content: Explain that a linear combination is a sum of scaled vectors (c1v1 + c2v2). 'Span' is the set of all reachable points. Visualize this as a 'coverage area' on a grid.
section_2.example: If the robot arm moves only along vector 'u', its span is a line. If it uses 'u' and 'v', its span is the entire 2D plane.

section_3.title: Linear Dependence: Redundancy
section_3.content: Define linear dependence as having 'extra' vectors that don't add new dimensions to the span. If one vector can be formed by the others, it is redundant.
section_3.example: Imagine three vectors pointing in the same direction. One vector is useful; the other two are redundant. The robot arm gains no new reach by adding them.

section_4.title: Bases: The Minimal Blueprint
section_4.content: Define a basis as a set of vectors that are linearly independent AND span the entire space. It is the 'minimal set' needed to describe any point in that space.
section_4.example: In a 2D room, two perpendicular unit vectors (i and j) form a basis. Every point in the room can be uniquely identified by their combination.

section_5.title: Summary and Visualization
section_5.content: Recap: Span (reach), Linear Dependence (redundancy), and Basis (the coordinate system). Emphasize that a basis is the most efficient language for a space.
section_5.example: Final Animation: An empty grid transforms as we add vectors; first a line (dependent), then a plane (spanning/basis). The grid lines shift to align with the chosen basis vectors.
